JUDGEMENT
PER HON’BLE MRS. SEEMA GUPTA, OFFICIATING CHAIRPERSON
1. The present batch of Appeals have been filed by Himachal Pradesh Power
Corporation Limited (“the Appellant”), assailing the orders dated 05.06.2024
(herein referred as “Impugned Orders”) passed by Himachal Pradesh Electricity
Regulatory Commission (hereinafter referred to as “HPERC/State
Commission”). The Impugned Orders pertains to the approval of capital cost,
including additional capitalization, and determination of tariff from the Commercial
Operation Date (“COD”) up to FY 2023–24 for three projects ( Sainj HEP – 2x50
MW, Kashang –I HEP 1x65 MW and Sawra Kuddu HEP – 3x37 MW) . The details
of the present Appeals are set out hereinbelow:
Page 4 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 89, 94 & 135 of 2025
Sl. Appeal No. Details
1. 89 of 2025 Assailing Order dated 05.06.2024 in Petition no. 25 of
2024 for 2 X 50 MW Sainj Hydro Electric Project
2. 94 of 2025 Assailing Order dated 05.06.2024 in Petition No. 24 of
2024 for 1X65MW Kashang Hydro Electric Project
3. 135 of 2025 Assailing Order dated 05.06.2024 in Petition No. 26 of
2024 for 3 X 37 MW Sawra Kuddu Hydro Electric Project
DESCRIPTION OF PARTIES:
2. The Appellant- Himachal Pradesh Power Corporation Limited (HPPCL), is
a generating company under Section 2(28) of the Electricity Act, 2003 and
operates 3 hydro power stations including Sainj HEP (2X50 MW), Kashang HEP
(3 X 65 MW) and Sawra Kuddu HEP (3 X 37 MW).
3. Respondent No 1 is the Himachal Pradesh Electricity Regulatory
Commission (hereinafter referred as “ HPERC/State Commission”) exercising
the powers and discharging the functions under the provisions of Electricity Act,
2003.
4. Respondent No 2, the Himachal Pradesh State Electricity Board Ltd.
(“HPSEBL”) is formed after the reorganization of erstwhile Himachal Pradesh
State Electricity Board (HPSEB) under the Electricity Act, 2003, and is a
distribution licensee operating in the State of Himachal Pradesh.
Factual matrix of the Case:
5. The Appellant has developed three hydroelectric projects in Himachal
Pradesh under the Himachal Pradesh Clean Energy Development Investment
Program funded by the Asian Development Bank (“ADB”). The details of the said
Page 5 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 89, 94 & 135 of 2025
projects, along with their respective Commercial Operation Dates (“COD”), as
approved by the State Commission, are set out hereinbelow:
i. Sainj HEP (100 MW – 2x50 MW) in District Kullu. Both units
achieved actual COD on 04.09.2017, with COD approved by
HPERC as 04.09.2017.
ii. Kashang HEP (195 MW – 3x65 MW) in District Kinnaur. Units 1,
2 & 3 achieved actual COD on 31.03.2017, 01.09.2016 and
03.03.2017 respectively, with COD approved by HPERC as
31.03.2017.
iii. Sawra Kuddu HEP (111 MW – 3x37 MW) on Pabbar River in
Rohru & Jubbal Tehsils, District Shimla. COD approved by
HPERC as 21.01.2021
6. On 29.03.2023, a long-term PPAs were executed between HPPCL and
HPSEBL for sale of 100% of net saleable energy from Kashang HEP Stage-I
(1x65 MW), 50% of net saleable energy from Sainj HEP (2x50 MW), and 100%
of net saleable energy from Sawra Kuddu HEP ( 3x37 MW), effective 01.04.2023
till the useful life of the projects. The remaining 50% power from Sainj HEP was
tied up for sale to the World Bank.
7. HPPCL filed petitions No. 24 of 2024 on 24.06.2023 (Kashang HEP-1x65
MW), Petition No 26 of 2024 (Sawra Kuddu HEP-2x50MW) & Petition No 25 of
2024 (Sainj HEP-3x37MW) on 03.06.2023 seeking approval of capital cost,
additional capitalization and determination of tariff for these three HEPs from
COD to FY 2023-24.
Page 6 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 89, 94 & 135 of 2025
8. HPERC passed the Impugned Tariff Orders dated 05.06.2024 determining
capital cost and aggregate revenue requirement for all three HEPs. The approved
capital cost after deduction of 90% of the GoHP Loan is Rs. 357.83 crore for
Kashang HEP, Rs. 436.89 crore for Sainj HEP, and Rs. 942.18 crore for Sawra
Kuddu HEP.
9. HPPCL filed review petitions challenging the Impugned Tariff Orders on the
issue of HPERC treating 90% of the GoHP Loan as a ‘grant’ instead of loan and
deducting the same from the project capital cost for computation of debt, equity,
depreciation, return on equity, interest and financing charges. HPERC dismissed
the review petitions on 05.11.2024 for Kashang and Sainj HEPs and on
19.11.2024 for Sawra Kuddu HEP.
10. Aggrieved by the findings in the Impugned Tariff Orders and Review Orders,
HPPCL has filed the present appeals.
ANALYSIS AND DISCUSSION
11. The Appellant has raised several issues in all the three appeals, however
the issue of treatment of 90% of the GoHP Loan as ‘grant’ and its deduction from
capital cost for tariff determination is common to all three appeals. At the outset
it was submitted by Learned Counsel for the Appellant that present appeals may
be confined to the aspect of consideration of loan to the Appellant Company as
grant and liberty may be granted to raise balance issues by way of separate
Appeals.
Since, the only issue i.e “treatment of 90% of GoHP Loan amount as Grant and
deduction of the same from Capital Cost for computation of tariff” to be
Page 7 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 89, 94 & 135 of 2025
adjudicated in all the three appeals is common, all the three appeals are disposed
of by this common judgement. Accordingly, we heard Mr. Vishrov Mukharjee,
learned Counsel for the Appellant, Mr. Pradeep Mishra, learned counsel on behalf
of Respondent No 1- State Commission and Mr. Anand Ganeshan, learned
counsel on behalf of Respondent No 2-HPSEBL, written submissions filed by
parties and Impugned Order and other documents relevant for adjudicating the
issue.
Submissions Urged on behalf of Appellant
12. Learned counsel for the Appellant submitted that on 10.09.2008, the
Government of India (“GoI”) entered into a Framework Financing Agreement with
the Asian Development Bank (“ADB”), whereby ADB agreed to extend a
multilateral/multi-tranche financing facility amounting to USD 800 million to GoI
under the Himachal Pradesh Clean Energy Development Investment Program.
13. On 10.11.2008, The GoI and ADB executed a Loan Agreement for Tranche-
1 inter alia for civil works pertaining to one unit (65 MW) and the common
powerhouse for all units of Kashang HEP. Under the said Loan Agreement, ADB
agreed to lend an amount of USD 150 million to GoI with a repayment tenure of
20 years along with a grace period commencing from 10.11.2008 to 15.10.2013,
with the last instalment being payable on 15.04.2033. The said agreement further
provided that GoI shall pay interest to ADB at LIBOR + 0.60%, less a credit of
0.40%, on a semi-annual basis.
14. It is submitted that the said Loan Agreement specifically contemplated that
the proceeds of the loan would be made available by GoI to the Govt of Himachal
Pradesh (GoHP) and, thereafter, the GoHP to make available an amount of USD
147 million, being approximately 98% of the total loan amount, to HPPCL under
Page 8 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 89, 94 & 135 of 2025
arm’s length on-lending arrangements acceptable to both ADB and GoI. The
agreement further stipulated that the rights and obligations arising out of the On-
Lending Agreements could neither be assigned, amended, abrogated nor waived
except with the satisfaction and approval of ADB and GoI.
15. In furtherance of the policy of the GoI aimed at encouraging investment and
promoting development in special category states such as Himachal Pradesh,
the loan amounts received from ADB were released by GoI to the Government of
Himachal Pradesh on concessional terms, wherein 90% of the financial
assistance was treated as grant and the remaining 10% was treated as loan.
16. Subsequently, GoHP executed an On-Lending Agreement with HPPCL,
which specifically notes that GoI had obtained a loan facility of USD 800 million
from the ADB for financing part of the cost of Kashang, Sainj, Sawra Kuddu and
Shongng Karcham Hydro Electric Projects, and that the loan proceeds would be
transferred by GoI to GoHP, which would further transfer the same to HPPCL.
The said Agreement further provided that GoHP would make available the said
funds to HPPCL by way of a loan carrying simple interest at the rate of 10% per
annum, with interest being payable annually on or before 15th January of each
financial year and the repayment obligation towards interest commencing
immediately. It is also stipulated that HPPCL would repay the principal amount of
each tranche of the loan within a period of 10 years from the expiry of the
applicable grace period of 5 years, tranche-wise. The Agreement additionally
provided that GoHP would remain responsible for repayment of the loan to
GoI/ADB and that HPPCL would bear no direct liability towards GoI or ADB in that
regard.
Page 9 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 89, 94 & 135 of 2025
17. However, the State Commission in the Impugned Orders has deducted the
GoHP Loan amount from the approved Capital cost of the projects, which is ex
facie contrary to Regulations 10-C, 11 and 26(1) & (2) of the Hydro Tariff
Regulations, 2011. It is submitted that the amounts released by the GoHP to
HPPCL were not in the nature of consumer contribution, grant or subsidy, but
constituted a loan arrangement, inasmuch as the said amounts were repayable
by HPPCL together with interest at the rate of 10% per annum.
18. It is submitted that even pursuant to the Impugned Tariff Orders, HPPCL
wrote to GoHP highlighting the severe financial implications arising from the
Impugned Orders and requested either conversion of the GoHP loan into grant
or issuance of appropriate directions under Section 108 of the Electricity Act to
HPERC for treating the said amount as loan. However, vide letter dated
19.03.2025, GoHP rejected the said request and categorically reiterated that the
financial assistance extended to HPPCL would continue to be treated as a loan
and not as a grant.
19. Subsequently, GoHP continued to demand payments from HPPCL towards
the said loan, and HPPCL, in compliance thereof, made substantial payments
towards interest on the loan, including approximately Rs. 290.20 Crore paid as
on 31.12.2024. Vide letter dated 27.06.2025, GoHP directed HPSEB to adjust an
amount of Rs. 324.52 Crores, being the interest due from HPPCL, against the
subsidy payable by GoHP to HPSEB. Thereafter, on 24.10.2025 and 28.11.2025,
HPPCL made further payments aggregating to Rs. 500 Crore towards interest on
the said loan.
20. It is submitted that Section 61(d) of the Electricity Act mandates the
Commission to safeguard consumer interests while also ensuring recovery of
cost of electricity in a reasonable manner, whereas Section 61(g) mandates that
Page 10 of 21

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 89, 94 & 135 of 2025
the tariff should progressively reflect the cost of supply. It is settled law that while
protection of consumer interest is an important consideration, the same cannot
override the generator’s entitlement to recovery of its legitimate costs, as noted
in “Punjab State Power Corpn. Ltd. v. PSERC”, (2015) 7 SCC 387 & “BSES
Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission & Ors.”,
(2023) 4 SCC 788.
21. It is submitted that under the cost-plus tariff regime, all input costs relating
to generation, including Capex and Opex, are ordinarily treated as pass-through
components in tariff, subject to prudence check by the Commission. This
Tribunal, in various judgments, has held that tariff is a reflection of the actual cost
and unless any imprudence is established in the manner of incurring cost, the
expenditure claimed by the generating company under Section 62 of the
Electricity Act 2003 should be allowed and passed through in tariff, as also held
in “NTPC v. CERC” 2009 ELR (APTEL) 916.
22. Accordingly, in the absence of any imprudence by HPPCL in obtaining the
loan, HPERC ought to have treated the GoHP Loan as a ‘loan’ and not as a ‘Grant’
and allowed the same to be recovered through tariff. However, on account of the
Impugned Orders, HPPCL is not allowed to recover the cost of its generation,
which is contrary to the principles of project-specific cost-reflective tariff

36. It is of relevance to advert to the Himachal Pradesh Electricity Regulatory
Commission (Terms and Conditions for Determination of Hydro Generation Tariff)
Regulations, 2011 (“Hydro Regulation 2011”). The scheme of the Regulations
provides that the capital cost deployed in a project, after prudence check by the
State Commission, shall be considered in the ratio of 70% loan and 30% equity,
where actual equity deployed exceeds 30%, and not more than 30% equity
otherwise. The Regulations further stipulate that capital works undertaken by a
generating company utilizing grants received from the State or Central
Government, including funds received under various schemes, shall be classified
under the category of “Grants.” Regulation 10(C)(3) clarifies that capital works

37. Admittedly, the funds received by the Appellant for implementation of the
projects from the Government of Himachal Pradesh do not fall within any of the
categories contemplated under Regulation 10(C)(3). The financing arrangement
is in the form of a loan, carrying a contractual liability of repayment together with
interest at 10% per annum. Such funds cannot, by any interpretative device, be
re-characterized as grants.
38. Thus, treating the loan as grant on the premise that since Govt. of India
extended the ADB funds by way of grants to GoHP and the same should have
been extended by GoHP to the Appellant as Grant, is devoid of legal and
regulatory basis.”, On such erroneous premise, the State Commission proceeded
to reduce the admissible capital cost by the corresponding amount. This
approach is contrary to the express provisions of the Hydro Tariff Regulations,
2011, which mandate that, save and except for capital works financed through
grants, the capital cost is to be considered in the debt: equity ratio of 70:30, with
equity capped at maximum 30 %. Significantly, the Regulations do not contain
any provision permitting a loan, even provisionally, as grant, with corresponding
reduction in capital cost for determination of tariff. State Commission has not
referred to any provisions in the Regulations to this effect.
39. The methodology adopted by the State Commission in the Impugned Order,
whereby the loan advanced by the Government of Himachal Pradesh has been
provisionally treated as grant, is in clear contravention of the statutory framework.
Section 61 of the Electricity Act, 2003 mandates that while determining tariff, the

Commissions shall ensure that generation, transmission and supply of electricity
are conducted on commercial principles. The Commission is duty-bound to
safeguard consumer interests, but equally to ensure recovery of the legitimate
cost of electricity in a reasonable manner, with tariff progressively reflecting the
actual cost of supply. This has been categorially held by Hon’ble Supreme Court
in “Punjab State Power Corpn. Ltd. v. PSERC”; (2015) 7 SCC 387 & “BSES
Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission & Ors”;,
(2023) 4 SCC 788).
40. Tariff determination under Section 62 of the Act requires the Commission to
consider the total debt employed for construction of the project on the basis of
the loan agreements executed between the generating company and its lender,
subject to the debt-equity ratio prescribed under the applicable tariff regulations.
41. By treating the loan received for implementation of the projects as 90%
grant, the Commission has artificially lowered the tariff, thereby jeopardising the
Appellant’s ability to discharge its contractual obligations of servicing interest and
repaying principal under the Loan Agreement with the Government of Himachal
Pradesh.
42. While, the protection of consumer interest remains a paramount objective
under given framework, the same cannot be invoked to defeat or curtail a
generator’s statutory right to recover its legitimate costs. In a regulated regime,
the Commission is bound to act strictly in accordance with the governing
provisions of the Act and the Regulations framed thereunder. The Commission
cannot, under the guise of advancing consumer interest, disregard or deviate
from the express regulatory framework governing tariff determination. Any
departure from the prescribed mechanism can only be effected by way of a formal
amendment to the Regulations in accordance with law, and not otherwise.

43. We are in agreement with the submissions of the Appellant that allocation
of funds either by way of grant or loan is a policy decision of the Government.
The State Commission, exercising powers under Section 86 of the Act, has no
jurisdiction to question such policy decisions. It is a settled position of law that
Courts and Tribunals cannot interfere with policy decisions of the Government,
including those relating to allocation of funds and resources or grant of loans,
which fall squarely within the policy domain. The reliance has been placed on
(“Balco Employees Union (Regd.) vs. UOI & Ors”; (2002) 2 SCC 333, “Small
Scale Industrial Manufactures Asso. v. UOI”; (2021) 8 SCC 511; “Rahul
Mohod. v. Govt. of NCT Delhi & Ors”; 2023 SCC OnLine Del 5492), wherein it
has been observed that the court have consistently refrained from interfering with
economic decisions unless the economic decisions are violative of constitutional
or legal limits. In other words, it is not the court/tribunal duty to consider relative
merits of economic framework and to consider whether a wiser or better one can
be evolved. The issue, if any, of the Government of Himachal Pradesh passing
of funds received from the Government of India as loan to the Appellant is an
inter-se matter between the two Governments and the State Commission has no
jurisdiction to re-characterize such funds as grant for the purpose of Tariff
determination.
44. Accordingly, issue of treatment of loan as Grant and corresponding
reduction in Capital Cost cannot be sustained in law.
